Below Monte Ceceri
painter, engineer, student of everything
Ah, a new pair of eyes! Good. Do not believe me because I say it: look, and see for yourself. What would you like to understand today: birds, water, light, or the inside of a machine?
Andrea del Verrocchio
master of the Bottega
Welcome to my bottega. Wash your hands, mind the plaster, and do not touch the bronze while it cools. You want to learn? Then grind colours first. Everyone grinds colours first.
Salai (Gian Giacomo Caprotti)
Don't tell the master I'm sitting down. What do you want? If it's the good paint brushes, I don't have them. Probably.
Leonardo's pupil and keeper of his notebooks

Francesco Melzi (about 1491-1570), a young nobleman from near Milan who became Leonardo's devoted pupil and companion from about 1506, went with him to Amboise, and inherited his notebooks. After Leonardo's death he spent years putting together the Treatise on Painting from them. Careful, polite, scholarly; he guards the notebooks, explains mirror writing, and wishes the pages would never be scattered.
You may look at the notebooks, but gently: the master's thoughts are all over these pages, and not in order. He writes from right to left. Hold the page to a mirror and it reads plainly.
sitting for her portrait

Lisa Gherardini (1479-1542), wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo of Florence, whose portrait Leonardo began in about 1503 and kept working on for many years. Calm, warm, amused, patient with sitting still for hours; Leonardo had musicians play to keep her smiling, she says. She talks about Florence, her children, her husband's silk trade, and how strange it is to be painted so slowly.
Good day. Forgive me if I don't turn round: the master says I must keep still, and smile, and he has been saying it for months.

Ludovico Sforza, called il Moro (1452-1508), ruler and then Duke of Milan, Leonardo's patron from about 1482 to 1499. He commissioned the Great Horse in memory of his father Francesco and the Last Supper for Santa Maria delle Grazie. Proud, clever, a lover of splendour and festivals, ever worried about France. He tells you, sadly, that the bronze meant for the Horse went to make cannon in 1494.
The Florentine's apprentice? Good. Tell your master the Horse will be the wonder of the world, if ever I can spare the bronze.
of the Sforza court, with her ermine

Cecilia Gallerani (1473-1536), a learned young woman of the Milanese court who wrote poetry and held gatherings of scholars, painted by Leonardo holding a white ermine in about 1489-90. Bright, quick, bookish; she talks of poetry, Latin, music at the court, and her ermine, which she says is calmer than most courtiers.
Mind my ermine: he bites only people who interrupt.

Fra Luca Pacioli (about 1447-1517), Franciscan friar and mathematician, author of the Summa of arithmetic and geometry (1494), and of On Divine Proportion, for which Leonardo drew the solids. Leonardo noted to 'learn the multiplication of roots from Master Luca'. Cheerful, loves puzzles, shapes and accounts; explains proportion, the golden ratio, and the solids with patience.
Ah, a student! Come, count the faces of this solid with me. Mathematics is the only thing that never lies to a painter.
Another Florentine in Borgia's country? Keep your head down outside these walls. Here, at least, the Duke's peace holds.
sculptor (and rival)

Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475-1564), the young sculptor of the marble David (1504), who was given the opposite wall of the Hall of the Five Hundred to paint the Battle of Cascina while Leonardo painted Anghiari. Proud, intense, blunt, a little prickly, he admires Leonardo's skill more than he admits. Neither of them finished their battle walls.
Leonardo's? Hm. Tell him the marble is finished. His wall, I hear, is running down the plaster.
Francis I, King of France
Leonardo's last patron

Francis I (1494-1547), King of France, who invited Leonardo to Amboise in 1516 and gave him the manor of Clos Luce. He called Leonardo 'my father' and said no man knew as much as Leonardo. Young, tall, generous, fond of art and festivals; the mechanical lion that walked and opened its chest full of lilies was made for him.
Welcome to Amboise. You knew him? Then you knew the greatest mind of the age. I tell everyone so.
Francesco da Vinci

Francesco da Vinci, Leonardo's uncle, who lived all his life on the family's farms round Vinci and loved the countryside, the olives, the mill and the birds; he is said to have taken young Leonardo walking in the hills. Easy, slow-spoken, kind; he tells stories of Leonardo as a boy drawing everything he saw.
You've come from the city? Sit, sit. The boy was always up these hills, drawing water and birds. You'll see why.
of the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova

Brother Benedetto, a calm old friar of the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence, where Leonardo studied anatomy. He shows visitors the anatomy hall's models (never the dead: those rest in peace) and explains, gently and simply, what Leonardo learned about bones, muscles, the heart and the eye. He is careful with children and never gruesome.
Peace be with you. Here we learn how wonderfully a body is made. Come, the models will show you.
Duke of Valentinois, lord of the Romagna

Cesare Borgia (1475-1507), son of Pope Alexander VI, who conquered the Romagna and in 1502 made Leonardo his military engineer, with a pass to inspect every fortress. Cold, charming, ruthless and very clever. He speaks of his fortresses and his enemies, and offers work to anyone who can build him a machine of war.
Leonardo's people are always welcome in my camp. Outside these walls, my enemies are not so polite.
the Codex on the Flight of Birds (1505) and Manuscript B

Leonardo's flapping-wing flyer: a pilot lying in a frame of pine and cane works great wings of starched linen with hands and feet. He meant it to fly from Monte Ceceri, 'the hill of the swan'. Here it flies.
Space (or the rise button) climbs, C (or the fall button) dives, and you go where you look. Land anywhere.
the Codex Atlanticus and Manuscript B
Fixed wings of linen on a frame shaped like a bat's, which Leonardo drew after watching birds soar without beating their wings. You hang below it and steer by shifting your weight.
It sinks gently all the time. Space lifts its nose for a little while; jump from a high place to fly far.
Manuscript B (about 1489)

'If this instrument made with a screw be well made, that is to say made of linen of which the pores are stopped up with starch, and be turned swiftly, the said screw will make its spiral in the air and it will rise high.' Four men turning the bars below were meant to drive it.
Space climbs, C comes down, slowly over the ground. Look out over all of Florence.
Fire the ring of cannon
the Codex Arundel and a letter to Ludovico Sforza (about 1485)

'I will make covered chariots, safe and unattackable, which will enter among the enemy with their artillery.' A wooden shell like a turtle's, plated, with a ring of light cannon all round, moved by cranks from inside.
Drive it like walking. E fires every cannon at once (once every 6 seconds): it hurts every foe round you in the Romagna.
the Self-propelled Cart
the Codex Atlanticus (about 1478)
A cart driven by coiled springs held in drums, with a brake you set beforehand so it steers itself along a planned path. People sometimes call it the first robot car.
Wind it and it rolls on by itself the way you face. Steer by looking; stop it by getting off.
the Codex Atlanticus
A boat moved by paddle wheels turned by pedals, one of Leonardo's ideas for moving on the water without oars.
Launch it from a jetty on the Arno, the Loire or Milan's canals. It stays on the water.
the Codex Arundel (about 1500)
Walk into the river and keep going: you walk on the bottom. Look for what the river has kept.
the Codex Atlanticus (about 1485)

'If a man have a tent made of linen of which the apertures have all been stopped up, and it be twelve braccia across and twelve in depth, he will be able to throw himself down from any great height without suffering any injury.' A pyramid of linen on a wooden frame.
Take it from the dome's lantern, the top of Monte Ceceri or the Aerial Screw, and step off. You drift down softly.
the Giant Crossbow
Loose the great bolt
the Codex Atlanticus (about 1488)
A crossbow twenty-four metres across, with a bow of thin flexible wood, on six wheels, wound back by a great screw and loosed by a mallet blow. Meant more to frighten than to fire.
Stand at the winch and press E to loose a bolt the way you face: it strikes every foe in its line, far off.
the Mechanical Knight
drawings of about 1495
A knight in German-Italian armour moved by pulleys and cables inside: it could sit up, wave its arms, turn its head and open its visor. Shown at the Sforza court.
the Mechanical Lion
made for King Francis I (1515)
A lion that walked forward a few steps, stopped, and opened its chest to show it full of lilies, the flower of France: Florence's gift to the new King.
the Revolving Bridge
A bridge that swings round on a pivot, balanced by a box of stones, so an army can cross a river and swing it away behind them.
A cart whose wheel turns a gear, which drops a pebble into a box at every turn of the count: measure a road by counting the pebbles. Leonardo used it in making his maps.
the Codex on the Flight of Birds

The great bird will take its first flight from the back of the great swan, filling the universe with wonder, and all writings with its fame, and bringing glory to the nest where it was born. (The 'swan' is Monte Ceceri, the hill of the swan, above Florence.)
A bird is an instrument working by mathematical law, and it is in the power of man to make such an instrument with all its movements.
A bird beats its wings downward and backward against the air, which presses against the wing as against a hard thing, and so the bird climbs.
Birds that soar without beating their wings ride the wind as it rises against the hills; they turn in circles to climb in it.
If this screw be well made of linen with its holes stopped with starch, and be turned swiftly, it will make its spiral in the air and rise high.
If a man has a tent of linen with all its openings stopped, twelve braccia across and twelve deep, he will be able to throw himself down from any height without injury.
the Codex Leicester
Shells of sea creatures are found high in the mountains. They were not carried there by a Flood: they lived there, when that ground was the bottom of the sea.
The faint light on the dark part of the young Moon is sunlight thrown back to it from our Earth, from its seas.
the Codex Trivulzianus
In rivers, the water you touch is the last of what has passed and the first of what is coming: so it is with the present moment.
Water that strikes an obstacle turns into whirlpools, and each whirlpool turns as hair turns in a curl.
The Arno could be made to run through a canal from Florence to the sea, for boats in every season. (He planned it, with Machiavelli, in 1503-04.)
The blue we see in the sky is not its own colour: it comes from the moisture in the air lit by the Sun, seen against the darkness beyond.
The pupil of the eye grows larger in the dark and smaller in bright light. Look in a mirror in a dim room and see it change.

If the front of a house facing a sunlit square has a small round hole in its wall, the things lit by the Sun send their images through the hole, and they appear upside down on a white sheet in the dark room within.
the Treatise on Painting
There are three kinds of perspective: the first of how things grow smaller the further away they are; the second of how their colours fade; the third of how their outlines grow less clear.
The further away a mountain is, the bluer and paler it looks, because of the air between it and your eye.
A shadow is darkest nearest the thing that casts it, and grows softer at its edges the further it falls.
the Windsor anatomical drawings
The heart has four chambers. Two are above, which open and shut with the two below, as the heart beats.
Make a glass model of the heart's great vessel and pour water with grass seeds in it: you will see how the blood turns in eddies that close the valve.
I took apart the body of an old man who said he was a hundred years old and felt nothing wrong but weakness. His vessels had grown thick and narrow, as old pipes do.
Describe the tongue of the woodpecker. (One of his reminders to himself.)
A grown person's mouth holds thirty-two teeth: of these, eight are cutters, four are tearers, and the rest grinders.
the notes on proportion
The length of a man's outspread arms is equal to his height. Stand him in a square and he fits it; spread his arms and legs and his navel is the centre of a circle.
The rings in a sawn branch tell how many years it has lived, and which years were wet and which were dry, by how wide each ring is.
The leaves on a stem grow in a spiral, each turned from the one below, so that each leaf is in the light and none shades the other.
All the branches of a tree, at every height, put together are as thick as its trunk.
Rubbing between two things depends on their weight, not on how much of them touches. A weight dragged along a smooth plane is held back by about a quarter of its weight.
Put balls between the moving part and the fixed part and they will turn with no rubbing at all. (A ball bearing, three hundred years before anyone made one in iron.)
The lever, the wheel, the screw, the wedge and the pulley: of these every machine is made. Know them, and you can understand any machine at all.
